## What it is

Nearly three in four adults living with diabetes in the WHO African Region do not know they have it, which is the highest proportion globally (News Agency of Nigeria, 2026). In his message for World Diabetes Day on 14 November 2026, the WHO Regional Director for Africa gave an estimated 24.6 million adults aged 20 to 79 years with diabetes in the region in 2024, a figure projected to reach 59.5 million by 2050 (News Agency of Nigeria, 2026). Worldwide, the International Diabetes Federation counts 589 million adults with diabetes, and more than four in ten of them are unaware of it (Gulf Today, 2026). A further 635 million adults are at high risk of type 2 diabetes, and the 2026 campaign theme, "Early action on diabetes", centres on better early detection and timely access to quality care (Gulf Today, 2026).

## Why it matters

Late diagnosis lets complications arrive before treatment does, as up to half of people with type 2 diabetes already have complications when they are diagnosed (Gulf Today, 2026). The Zambian data fit this pattern, as the 2017 national STEPS survey of 3,608 adults aged 18 to 69 years found diabetes in 7.2% of participants (Pengpid & Peltzer, 2021). Among those with diabetes only 22.3% were aware of it and 9.4% were taking treatment, while only 8.4% of all participants had ever had their blood glucose examined by a health worker (Pengpid & Peltzer, 2021). Testing was more than twice as common in urban areas (11.8%) as in rural areas (5.4%) (Pengpid & Peltzer, 2021).

## What to remember

We should read the regional and Zambian figures as different measures, because the regional figure is an estimate for the whole African Region while the STEPS survey measured awareness among Zambian adults in 2017. The WHO message points to the WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable Diseases, the HEARTS-D package for type 2 diabetes and the PEN-Plus strategy for severe noncommunicable diseases at first-level referral facilities (News Agency of Nigeria, 2026). Rwanda has achieved nationwide district-level coverage of PEN-Plus, although gaps remain in trained health workers, diagnostics, essential medicines and continuous care (News Agency of Nigeria, 2026). Type 2 diabetes can develop without obvious symptoms, so people at higher risk need regular screening. The Regional Director also listed increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, persistent tiredness and blurred vision as warning signs that should prompt testing (News Agency of Nigeria, 2026).
